title: S1 — Soils, Rock Bearing, and Compaction Theory
summary: Why fill gets compacted, what the Proctor test actually establishes, why lift thickness is non-negotiable, and what your limestone's superb bearing does and doesn't guarantee. PLAIN: squeezed-out air makes fill strong. PRO: percent of maximum dry density at optimum moisture, verified per lift.

sections.heading: Why compaction exists
sections.body: PLAIN: Loose fill is mostly air pockets, and air carries nothing — a building on loose fill settles as the air squeezes out over years. Compaction squeezes the air out NOW, with a roller, so the particles lock together before anything is built on them. Water matters both ways: too dry and friction keeps particles from packing; too wet and water fills the voids and the fill pumps like a waterbed under the roller. PRO: The reference is the Proctor test — the lab finds the fill's maximum dry density and optimum moisture content (OMC); the field spec is a percentage of that maximum, typically 95% Standard Proctor for general fill and 98% (or 95% Modified) under structures and pavements. Verified by nuclear density gauge or sand cone at a set frequency — one test per 2,500–5,000 sf per lift, failed areas retested after rework.

sections.heading: Lift discipline and the rock-fill traps
sections.body: PLAIN: Rollers only compact the top portion of what they roll — dump three feet of fill and roll it beautifully, and only the top foot is dense; the rest is future settlement with a nice surface. So fill goes in thin horizontal layers — lifts — of 8–12 inches loose, each rolled and tested before the next. PRO: 'Place it in lifts' is the first sentence of every fill spec; thicker lifts only with heavy vibratory equipment and the engineer's written approval. Your crushed limestone is angular and free-draining — it compacts superbly under a vibratory smooth-drum roller (sheepsfoot is for clays you don't have). Two traps: OVERSIZE — chunks bigger than ~2/3 the lift thickness bridge and hide voids that collapse later, so spec a max particle size and crush to it; and KARST — a passing density test on fill above a hidden void proves nothing about the void, which is why probing/proof-rolling the subgrade comes BEFORE fill.

sections.heading: Bearing on rock: capacity isn't the question
sections.body: PLAIN: Intact Bahamian limestone can carry ten times more than any house pushes into it — the danger is never the rock that's there, it's the spots where it isn't: weathered zones, cavities, loose sand pockets. PRO: allowable bearing on sound limestone runs 10,000–40,000+ psf against a house's ~2,000–3,000 psf demand — the geotech's job is finding the EXCEPTIONS. Standard practice: probe footing excavations (percussion probe or air track) and remediate cavities by excavate-and-replace with lean concrete ($180–260/cy) or grout. This is Module 1's karst lesson at footing scale.

quiz.teach: Density tests measure the material the gauge can reach — roughly the top of the lift.
quiz.prompt: Density tests pass at 95% Proctor, but you learn the fill was placed in 24-inch lifts instead of the specified 8–12. Accept or reject?

choices.text: Reject — the tests only prove the top of each lift; the bottom half of every 24-inch lift is uncompacted fill wearing a passing certificate
choices.why: Correct. The roller's energy doesn't reach the bottom of a thick lift; the passing tests are sampling exactly the material that DID get compacted.

choices.text: Accept — 95% is 95%, however it was placed
choices.why: The 95% describes where the gauge probe reached, not the buried bottom half. Lift thickness is HOW the spec guarantees full-depth density.

choices.text: Accept with extra tests on the surface
choices.why: More tests at the same depth measure the same top slice. The problem is below the gauge's reach — only removal and re-placement in proper lifts fixes it.

choices.text: Accept if the contractor warranties settlement
choices.why: A warranty on hidden loose fill is a promise to argue later. The physics doesn't negotiate: unrolled fill settles under load.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a beautifully rolled 3-ft dump of fill is a future settlement claim. PRO: 'place and compact in maximum 12-inch loose lifts, test per lift' — the lift discipline IS the compaction spec; density numbers without it are theater. (S1)

quiz.teach: The Proctor test establishes the reference: this material's maximum dry density and its optimum moisture content.
quiz.prompt: The contractor wants to skip the Proctor test on crushed rock 'because it always passes.' Why does the reference test still matter?

choices.text: Without a lab maximum there is no pass/fail criterion — '95% of maximum' is meaningless with no maximum, and you've surrendered your leverage on every future density dispute
choices.why: Correct. Field tests report percent of the Proctor maximum. No Proctor, no denominator, no enforceable spec.

choices.text: It doesn't — crushed limestone genuinely always passes
choices.why: It usually compacts well, which is exactly why the contractor wants to skip the $ few hundred that makes 'well' verifiable and enforceable.

choices.text: The Proctor tells you which roller to use
choices.why: Equipment selection follows material type; the Proctor's real product is the NUMBER every field test is measured against.

choices.text: It's required for the building permit only
choices.why: MOW may want records, but the owner-side reason is contractual: the reference converts 'looks compacted' into a measured criterion.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: you can't grade a test without an answer key — the Proctor is the answer key. PRO: 'no max density = no pass/fail criterion = no leverage.' The lab work is cheap; the argument it prevents is not. (S1)

quiz.teach: A proof roll drives a loaded truck slowly across the subgrade while you watch how the ground responds.
quiz.prompt: The proof roll reveals a soft, pumping zone in otherwise sound rock subgrade. What's the correct sequence?

choices.text: Investigate the DEPTH of the soft zone first (probe it), then choose undercut-and-replace vs grout on what the probing shows
choices.why: Correct. The remedy depends entirely on how deep the problem goes — undercutting 2 ft of soft pocket is routine; a karst throat needs grouting. Diagnose before prescribing.
Undercutting without probing might chase a karst feature downward indefinitely, or waste money over-excavating a shallow lens. The probe costs an hour.

choices.text: Add more fill on top to bridge it
choices.why: Burying a pumping zone converts a visible problem into a hidden one under your road — the differential-settlement crack arrives on schedule (V3-4).

choices.text: Roll it more until it stops pumping
choices.why: Pumping means water and fines are moving underground — more energy makes it worse, not denser. The roller is telling you something is wrong DOWN there.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the pumping ground is a message from below — read it before fixing it. PRO: 'proof roll, map the soft zones, probe for depth, then undercut or grout per the geotech.' Proof-rolling before fill is the cheap insurance that makes every later density test mean something. (S1)

quiz.teach: Say it like a pro: field vocabulary is precision, not jargon.
quiz.prompt: Which instruction is the correctly-specified version of 'compact the fill properly under the building pads'?

choices.text: 'Structural fill in 8–12 inch loose lifts, compacted to 98% Standard Proctor at ±2% of optimum moisture, one density test per 2,500 sf per lift'
choices.why: Correct — material, lift thickness, density criterion, moisture window, and verification frequency. Every word is enforceable.

choices.text: 'Compact thoroughly with appropriate equipment to engineer's satisfaction'
choices.why: Nothing here can be measured or failed — 'thoroughly' and 'appropriate' are dispute-generators dressed as diligence.
Method specs (passes) without a density criterion certify effort, not result. Passes vary with material and moisture; density is the product.
Closer — but without lift thickness and test frequency, 98% is unverifiable at depth (see the 24-inch-lift trap).

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a good spec says what, how thick, how dense, how wet, and how you'll check. PRO: density criterion + lift discipline + moisture window + test frequency — the four-part sentence every earthworks contract needs. (S1)

mathProblems.title: Density tests for a pad program
mathProblems.context: Test count math: pad area ÷ coverage per test, per lift, then lifts. Treat 'tests needed' as the crew-days quantity: each area unit at the coverage rate needs one test.

mathProblems.title: Cavity remediation
mathProblems.context: Probing found cavities under footings; the remedy is excavate-and-replace with lean concrete, priced per cubic yard.

decisionPoints.title: The always-passes argument
decisionPoints.scenario: Week one of pad fill. The earthworks contractor proposes skipping the Proctor and cutting test frequency in half: 'crushed limestone always passes, you're paying the lab to tell you what everyone knows.' Your testing lab budget line is visible in this month's cost report; the fill will be invisible under 302 houses forever.

options.label: Run the full program: Proctor reference, specified lift checks, full test frequency — and share the results dashboard with the contractor
options.outcome: The lab costs what it costs. In month three a batch of fill from the new crusher screen runs wet and fails four tests — caught, dried, re-rolled the same week. That's the program paying for itself: the point was never that fill usually passes; it's catching the batch that doesn't.

options.label: Keep the Proctor but halve the test frequency
options.outcome: The reference survives but the sampling net is now twice as coarse — a failing area has even odds of never being tested. Defensible on low-risk general fill; under structures, the saved money is measured against invisible foundations.

options.label: Skip the Proctor, spot-test occasionally
options.outcome: Without the reference maximum, your occasional tests report percentages of nothing. When settlement cracks appear in year two, the contractor's defense writes itself: 'no spec was established.' You built the argument you'll lose.

decisionPoints.debrief: Verification programs exist for the exception, not the rule — crushed limestone passing 95 times out of 100 is exactly why the 5 need catching. And the Proctor is the answer key: skip it and every future density number is an opinion. (S1)
